list.listitem: Organic disease is uncommon; a community-based study with consistent evaluation of organic etiologies has not been performed to date.C

Diagnosis is predominantly clinical; colic is usually defined as unexplained paroxysmal bouts of fussing and crying in infants younger than 6 months of age that last more than 3 hours a day, occur on more than 3 days a week, and are present for more than 3 weeks of duration.C
Consider dietary changes and behavioral interventions, although the evidence is weak.B
Probiotics, including lactobacillus reuteri and bifidobacterium animalis subsp. lactis, appear to be somewhat effective.B
Parental support is paramount as the risk of physical abuse is increased in colicky infants.C

background.definition: The most widely accepted definition of colic is "Wessel's Rule of 3's": unexplained paroxysmal bouts of fussing and crying in infants younger than 6 months of age that last more than 3 hours a day, occur on more than 3 days a week, and are present for more than 3 weeks of duration.

list.listitem: Varies widely as definitions often change. A systematic review cited 3% to 28% occurrence rate.
One of the most frequent complaints brought to a physician in an infant's first 3 months of life.
Excessive crying is recognized as a risk factor for potentially fatal child abuse.
Unknown; generally considered a behavioral syndrome.
Organic disease identified in less than 5% of infants.
Increased risk with first-born child.
Gender, socioeconomic status, type of feeding, parental smoking, and family history of atopy do not increase risk.
Unknown.

A case-control study found Helicobacter pylori associated with colic (OR: 15.3; 95% CI: 17.9-29.8). A different case control study found that the intestinal microbiota of infants with colic was different than control infants, with 2x more proteobacteria.

Diagnosis is made clinically: unexplained paroxysmal bouts of fussing and crying in infants younger than 6 months of age that last more than 3 hours a day, occur on more than 3 days a week, and are present for more than 3 weeks of duration.C
Studies generally agree that infants with colic are healthy, thriving, and below 6 months of age.C

Differential.Differential_Features: Otoscopic examination with erythematous, bulging, nonmobile tympanic membrane
Fluorescein examination reveals a corneal abrasion
Fluorescein examination reveals a foreign body in eye
Hair wrapped around digit or other body part
History of constipation, stool felt in abdomen or seen on KUB
Vomiting, currant jelly stools, periods of crying followed by periods of lethargy
Lethargy, full fontanelle, abnormal neuro examination, fever
History of direct ingestion or maternal ingestion if breastfed

list.listitem: Colic typically occurs in healthy, thriving infants younger than 6 months of age. It is characterized by excessive time spent crying with paroxysms of fussing or crying lasting up to several hours. Often characterized as inconsolable or high-pitched. Associated findings may include facial flushing, circumoral pallor, back arching, clenching of the hands, legs drawn up, or extended, cold feet.
Symptoms usually peak at about 6 weeks of age (see ). Episodes are usually diurnal, occuring in the early morning and late evening hours.
Associated GI symptoms may include tension or distension of the abdomen; passing feces or flatus may or may not provide relief.
Evaluate maternal characteristics, including screening for anxiety or depression.
Obtain UA and/or urine culture to rule out UTI, especially if the patient is an uncircumcised male.
Otherwise, diagnostic tests are only recommended if clinically indicated based on history and physical examination.
See for a suggested approach to the child with acute, persistent crying.
No consistently effective intervention is available.B
If breast-feeding, can consider hypoallergenic diet for mother or giving herbal tea.B
If formula-fed, can consider change to soy or hypoallergenic formula or giving herbal tea.B
Decreased stimulation may also be effective.B
Probiotics, including lactobacillus reuteri and bifidobacterium animalis subsp. lactis, appear to be somewhat effective at reducing daily crying time.B
Although shown to be beneficial, dicyclomine (Bentyl) was given a black box warning by the manufacturer for use in infants younger than 6 months old.
Simethicone (Mylicon, Gas-X) is likely not beneficial.
There is limited evidence that dietary interventions may be beneficial (hypoallergenic maternal diet if breast-feeding and soy or hypoallergenic formula if formula-fed).

A maternal diet low in FODMAP (fermentable oligosaccharides, disaccharides, monosaccharides and polyols) resulted in a small improvement in crying time (32% reduction vs 20% reduction) when compared with usual diet in a small (n = 40) unblinded randomized trial.
Herbal teas may be beneficial.
A meta-analysis concluded that the evidence for lactase, sucrose, and glucose is weak. A single RCT concluded that sucrose may have a short-lived positive response.

A Cochrane review identified 15 RCTs of dietary manipulation therapies for colic, but concluded that the low quality and inconsistency of studies precluded them from recommending any specific therapy.
A small (n = 40) crossover randomized trial concluded that white noise was more effective than swinging for colic.
Acupuncture is not recommended based on systematic reviews.

Manipulative therapy (chiropratic, osteopathic and cranial manipulation) may decrease crying by an hour and 12 minutes per day (mean difference −1.2; 95% CI: −2.2 to −0.3). However, the positive studies were at high risk of performance bias since the assessors (parents) were not blind to who received the intervention. When the meta-analysis was restricted only to those studies at low risk of performance bias, the difference was no longer statistically significant.Another systematic review of 5 studies with 422 babies found no benefit to osteopathic or chiropractic manipulation, with the quality of evidence low or very low.
Probiotics appear to have some benefit, particularly for reducing crying time.

A Cochrane review concluded that daily crying time is reduced with probiotics, with the greatest benefit from Lactobacillus reuteri. Similarly, a systematic review of 15 RCTs concluded that probiotics fed to breast fed infants with colic reduced crying time approximately 50% compared with placebo.

There is some evidence that the specific probiotic utilized matters. The specific probiotic lactobacillus reuteri was found to be effective in a meta-analysis of 4 double-blinded RCTs with 345 infants, with a mean reduction in crying time at 21 days of 25 minutes (95% CI: 3.5-47.5 minutes) and a greater likelihood of treatment success (RR 1.7; 95% CI: 1.4-2.2). This was confirmed in a subsequent meta-analysis.

Results in individual trials varied. In another double-blinded RCT of 80 infants, daily treatment with Bifidobacterium animalis subsp lactis was found to be effective, with 80% of treated infants experiencing at least a 50% reduction in average daily crying duration within 28 days, compared to only 33% of untreated infants (p <0.0001). However, an RCT of more than 900 pregnant mothers and subsequently their infants randomized to a mix of 3 probiotics (Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG and LC705, Bifidobacterium breve Bb99, and Propionibacterium freudenreichii ssp shermanii) found no difference in the likelihood of colic.

Must reassure and partner with parents regarding infant crying. A Cochrane review concluded that while the quality of evidence was low, parental training programs appear to reduce crying times compared with control. Elements employed in various studies included soothing techniques, general care and feeding advice, stress reduction and empathy for parents, and positive play interaction advice.

A crossover trial evaluated different approaches for promoting sleep in a crying infant. According to this small study, the best approach to a crying infant seems to be walking while holding the baby for 5 minutes followed by another 5 to 8 minutes of sitting and holding the baby before placing the baby in a bed. Just sitting with a crying baby did not calm them, and you can forget about putting a crying baby directly into a bed.
Car ride simulators have not been shown to be beneficial.
Decreasing infant stimulation may be beneficial.
REST routine (Reassurance, Empathy, Support, Time Out) may help provide relief to families.
Screen for postpartum depression.
Ultimately self-resolving condition, not lasting beyond 6 months of age.C
Two prospective cohort studies of infants with and without colic found no long-term behavioral effects of colic.B
Excessive crying is recognized as a risk factor for potentially fatal child abuse.C
A case-control study found that children with migraine were more likely to have had infantile colic than those without migraine (OR: 6.6; 95% CI: 4.4-10.0).C

cell.label: Infant with acute excessive crying. Perform history and physical examination. Cause identified?
Follow 24 hours in hospital or at home; consider idiopathic crying episode.
Consider: radiologic studies, chemistry tests, pulse oximetry, toxicology tests, and/or lumbar puncture based on history and physical.
Continue observation, in hospital, until crying stops or diagnosis made.
